Learning Strategy to Classify Parkinson's
Disease from Speech in Three Different
Languages
J. C. Vasquez-Correa1,2, T. Arias-Vergara1,2,3, C. D. Rios-Urrego2, M.
Schuster?, J. Rusz4, J. R. Orozco-Arroyavel,2, E. Noth1
1Pattern Recognition Lab. Friedrich-Alexander Universitat, Erlangen-Nürnberg,
Feb 2020 Germany
2 Faculty of Engineering. Universidad de Antioquia UdeA, Calle 70 No. 52-21,
Medellin,Colombia

Abstract.Parkinson's disease patients develop different speech impair-
ments that affect their communication capabilities. The automatic as-
sessment of the speech of the patients allows the development of com-
puter aided tools to support the diagnosis and the evaluation of the
disease severity. This paper introduces a methodology to classify Parkin-
son's disease from speech in three different languages: Spanish, German,
and Czech. The proposed approach considers convolutional neural net-
works trained with time frequency representations and a transfer learning
strategy among the three languages. The transfer learning scheme aims
arXiv:2002.04374v1 to improve the accuracy of the models when the weights of the neural network are initialized with utterances from a different language than
the used for the test set. The results suggest that the proposed strat-
egy improves the accuracy of the models in up to 8% when the base
model used to initialize the weights of the classifier is robust enough.
In addition, the results obtained after the transfer learning are in most
cases more balanced in terms of specificity-sensitivity than those trained
without the transfer learning strategy.
Keywords: Parkinson's Disease · Speech Processing · Convolutional
Neural Networks· Transfer Learning
1 Introduction
Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the
progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the mid-brain producing several mo-
tor and non-motor impairments in the patients[1].Motor symptoms include

2 J.C.Vasquez-Correaet al.
among others, bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, micrographia, and different
speech impairments. The speech impairments observed in PD patients are typ-
ically grouped as hypokinetic dysarthria, and include symptoms such as vocal
folds rigidity, bradykinesia, and reduced control of muscles and limbs involved in
the speech production. The effects of dysarthria in the speech of PD patients in-
clude increased acoustic noise, reduced intensity, harsh and breathy voice quality,
increased voice nasality, monopitch, monoludness, speech rate disturbances, im-
precise articulation of consonants [2], and involuntary introduction of pauses [3].
Clinical observations in the speech of patients can be objectively and automati-
cally measured by using computer aided methods supported in signal processing
and pattern recognition with the aim to address two main aspects: (1) to sup-
port the diagnosis of the disease by classifying healthy control (HC) subjects and
patients, and (2) to predict the level of degradation of the speech of the patients
according to a specific clinical scale.
Most of the studies in the literature to classify PD from speech are based
on computing hand-crafted features and using classifiers such as support vector
machines (SVMs) or K-nearest neighbors (KNN). For instance, in [4],the au-
thors computed features related to perturbations of the fundamental frequency
and 20 HC subjects, Turkish speakers. Classifiers based on KNN and SVMs
were considered, and accuracies of up to 75% were reported. Later, in [5] the
authors proposed a phonation analysis based on several time frequency repre-
sentations to assess tremor in the speech of PD patients. The extracted features
were based on energy and entropy computed from time frequency representa-
tions. Several classifiers were used, including Gaussian mixture models (GMMs)
and SVMs.Accuracies of up to 77% were reported in utterances of the PC-GITA
database [6], formed with utterances from 50 PD patients and 50 HC subjects,
Colombian Spanish native speakers. The authors from [7] computed features to
model different articulation deficits in PD such as vowel quality,coordination
of laryngeal and supra-laryngeal activity, precision of consonant articulation,
tongue movement, occlusion weakening, and speech timing. The authors studied
the rapid repetition of the syllables /pa-ta-ka/ pronounced by 24 Czech native
speakers, and reported an accuracy of 88% discriminating between PD patients
and HC speakers, using an SVM classifier. Additional articulation features were
proposed in [8], where the authors modeled the difficulty of PD patients to
start/stop the vocal fold vibration in continuous speech. The model was based
on the energy content in the transitions between unvoiced and voiced segments.
The authors classified PD patients and HC speakers with speech recordings in
three different languages (Spanish, German, and Czech), and reported accuracies
ranging from 80% to 94% depending on the language; however, the results were
optimistic, since the hyper-parameters of the classifier were optimized based on
the accuracy on the test set. Another articulation model was proposed in [9]. The
authors considered a forced alignment strategy to segment the different phonetic
units in the speech utterances. The phonemes were segmented and grouped to
train different GMMs. The classification was performed based on a threshold of

CNNs and a Transfer Learning Strategy to Classify PD from Speech 3
the difference between the posterior probabilities from the models created for
HC subjects and PD patients. The model was tested with Colombian Spanish
utterances from the PC-GITA database[6] and with the Czech data from[10].
The authors reported accuracies of up to 81% for the Spanish data, and of up
to 94% for the Czech data.
In addition to the hand-crafted feature extraction models,there is a grow-
ing interest in the research community to consider deep learning models in the
assessment of the speech of PD patients [11,12,13]. Deep learning methods have
the potential to extract more abstract and robust features than those manu-
ally computed.These features could help toimprove the accuracy of different
models to classify pathological speech, such as PD [14]. A deep learning based
articulation model was proposed in [12] to model the difficulties of the patients
to stop/start the vibration of the vocal folds. Transitions between voiced and
unvoiced segments were modeled with time-frequency representations and con-
volutional neural networks (CNNs). The authors considered speech recordings of
PD patients and HC speakers in three languages: Spanish, German, and Czech,
and reported accuracies ranging from 70% to 89%, depending on the language.
However, in a language independent scenario, i.e., training the CNN with utter-
ances from one language and testing with the remaining two, the results were
not satisfactory (accuracy< 60%).
The classification of PD from speech in different languages has to be carefully
conducted to avoid bias towards the linguistic content present in each language.
For instance, Czech and German languages are richer than Spanish language
in terms of consonant production, which may cause that it is easier to produce
consonant sounds by Czech PD patients than by Spanish PD patients. Despite
these language dependent issues, the results in the classification of PD in dif-
ferent languages could be improved using a transfer learning strategy among
languages, i.e., to train a base model with utterances from one language, and
then,to perform a fine-tuning of the weights with utterances from the target
language [15]. Similar approaches based on transfer learning have been recently
considered to classify PD using handwriting [16]. In the present study, we pro-
pose a methodology to classify PD via a transfer learning strategy with the aim
to improve the accuracy in different languages. CNNs trained with utterances
from PD patients in a different language. The models are evaluated with speech
utterances in Spanish, German, and Czech languages. The results suggest that
the use of a transfer learning strategy improved the accuracy of the models over
8%with respect to those obtained when the model is trained only with utterance
from the target language.
2Materials and methods
2.1Data
Speech recordings of patients in three different languages are considered: Spanish,
German, and Czech. All of the recordings were captured in noise controlled

conditions. The speech signals were down-sampled to 16kHz. The patients in
the three datasets were evaluated by a neurologist expert according to the third
section of the movement disorder society, unified Parkinson's disease rating scale
(MDS-UPDRS-II) [17]. Table 1 summarizes the information about the patients
and healthy speakers.
Spanish The Spanish data consider the PC-GITA corpus [6], which contains
utterances from 50 PD patients and 50 HC,Colombian Spanish native speakers.
The participants were asked to pronounce a total of 10 sentences, the rapid
repetition of /pa-ta-ka/,/pe-ta-ka/,/pa-ka-ta/,/pa/,/ta/,and /ka/,one text
with 36 words, and a monologue. All patients were in ON state at the time of
the recording, i.e., under the effect of their daily medication.
many are considered [18]. The participants performed four speech task: the rapid
repetition of /pa-ta-ka/, 5 sentences, one text with 81 words, and a monologue.
Czech A total of 100 native Czech speakers (50 PD,50 HC) were considered [19].
The speech tasks performed by the participants include the rapid repetition of
the syllables /pa-ta-ka/, a read text with 80 words, and a monologue.

2.2 2Segmentation
Speech signals are analyzed based on the automatic detection of onset and offset
transitions, which model the difficulties of the patients to start /stop the move-
ment of the vocal folds. The detection of the transitions is based on the presence
of the fundamental frequency of speech in short-time frames, as it was shown

CNNs and a Transfer Learning Strategy to Classify PD from Speech 5
in [8]. The border between voiced and unvoiced frames is detected, and 80 ms of
the signal are taken to the left and to the right, forming segments with 160 ms
length. The transition segments are modeled with two different approaches: (1)
a baseline model based on hand-crafted features, which are classified using an
SVM, and (2) a model based on time-frequency representations used as input to
train a CNN, which then will be used for the transfer learning strategy. Further
details are given in the following subsections.
2.3Baseline model
The features extracted from the transitions include 12 Mel-Frequency Cepstral
Coefficients (MFCCs) with their first and second derivatives, and the log energy
of the signal distributed into 22 Bark bands. The total number of descriptors
corresponds to 58. Four statistical functionals (mean,standard deviation, skew-
ness, and kurtosis) are computed for each descriptor, obtaining a 232-dimensional
feature-vector per utterance. The classification of PD patients and HC speak-
ers is performed with a radial basis SVM with margin parameter C = 10 and
a Gaussian kernel with parameter  = 0.0001. The SVM is tested following a
10-fold Cross-Validation strategy, speaker independent.
2.4CNN model
to discriminate between PD patients and HC subjects.The STFT with 256 fre-
quency bins is computed for each segmented transition, for a window length of
16 ms and a step-size of 4 ms, forming 41 time frames per transition. The ob-
tained spectrogram is transformed into the Mel-scale using 80 filters, forming
an spectrogram with a size of 80x41,which is used to train the CNNs. The
architecture of the implemented CNN is summarized in Table 2. It consists of
four convolutional and max-pooling layers, dropout to regularize the weights,
and two fully connected layers followed by the output layer to make the final
decision using a softmax activation function. The number of feature maps on
each convolutional layer is twice the previous one in order to get more detailed
representations of the input space in the deeper layers. The CNN is trained using
the the cross-entropy as the loss function, using an Adam optimizer [20].
2.5Transfer learning
Transfer learning allows to use a neural network trained for one task to be used
in another domain.We use transfer learning to classify patients and healthy
speakers in three different languages. The CNN architecture described before is
used to train a CNN with utterances from one language. Then, the pre-trained
model is used as a base to initialize two different models with the remaining
languages. Figure 1 summarizes this procedure.

3 Experiments and results
The experiments are divided as follows: First, the baseline and the CNN models
are trained considering each language individually. Then, the trained CNNs for
each language are used as a base model in the transfer learning strategy in
order to improve the accuracy in the other two languages. All speech exercises
performed by the participants were considered for the classification strategy. The
final decision for each speaker was obtained by a majority voting strategy among
the differentspeechexercises.

4 Conclusion
This study proposed the use of a transfer learning strategy based on fine-tuning
to classify PD from speech in three different languages: Spanish, German, and
Czech. The transfer learning among languages aimed to improve the accuracy
when the models are initialized with utterances from a different language than
the one used for the test set. Mel-scale spectrograms extracted from the transi-
tions between voiced and unvoiced segments are used to train a CNN for each
language. Then, the trained models are used to fine-tune a model to classify
utterances in the remainingtwolanguages.
The results indicate that the transfer learning among languages improved
the accuracy of the models in up to 8% when a base model trained with Spanish

CNNs and a Transfer Learning Strategy to Classify PD from Speech 9
utterances is used to fine-tune a model to classify PD German utterances. The
results obtained after the transfer learning are also more balanced in terms of
specificity-sensitivity and have a lower variance. In addition, the transfer learning
among languages scheme was accurate to improve the accuracy in the target
language only when the base model was robust enough. This was observed when
the model trained with Spanish utterances was used to initialize the models for
German and Czechlanguages.
Further experiments will include the development of more robust base mod-
els using hyper-parameter optimization strategies like those based on Bayesian
optimization. In addition, the base models will be trained considering two of the
languages instead of only one of them. The trained models will also be evaluated
to classify the speech of PD patients in several stages of the disease based on the
MDS-UPDRS-III score, or based on their dysarthria severity [21]. Further exper-
iments will also include transfer learning among diseases, for instance training
a base model with utterances to classify PD,and use such a model to initialize
another one to classify other neurological diseases such as Hungtinton's disease.

The study uses speech recordings of patients in three different languages: Spanish, German, and Czech. The Spanish data come from the PC-GITA corpus. PC-GITA contains utterances from 50 PD patients and 50 HC, Colombian Spanish native speakers. The Spanish dataset speaker composition is therefore 50 PD patients and 50 healthy control speakers, Colombian Spanish native speakers. This corpus provides the Spanish portion of the cross-lingual speech data.

The German data consist of speech recordings of 44 PD patients and 44 HC speakers. The German dataset description reports this composition. The Czech dataset contains a total of 100 native Czech speakers, comprising 50 PD patients and 50 healthy controls. These datasets supply speech recordings of Parkinson’s disease patients and healthy controls across multiple languages. Abstract.Parkinson's disease patients develop different speech impair-
ments that affect their communication capabilities. The automatic as-
sessment of the speech of the patients allows the development of com-
puter aided tools to support the diagnosis and the evaluation of the
disease severity. This paper introduces a methodology to classify Parkin-
son's disease from speech in three different languages: Spanish, German,
and Czech. The proposed approach considers convolutional neural net-
works trained with time frequency representations and a transfer learning
strategy among the three languages. The transfer learning scheme aims

the used for the test set. The results suggest that the proposed strat-
egy improves the accuracy of the models in up to 8% when the base
model used to initialize the weights of the classifier is robust enough.
In addition, the results obtained after the transfer learning are in most

1 Introduction
Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the
progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the mid-brain producing several mo-
tor and non-motor impairments in the patients[1].Motor symptoms include

2 J.C.Vasquez-Correaet al.
among others, bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, micrographia, and different
speech impairments. The speech impairments observed in PD patients are typ-
ically grouped as hypokinetic dysarthria, and include symptoms such as vocal
folds rigidity, bradykinesia, and reduced control of muscles and limbs involved in
the speech production. The effects of dysarthria in the speech of PD patients in-
clude increased acoustic noise, reduced intensity, harsh and breathy voice quality,
increased voice nasality, monopitch, monoludness, speech rate disturbances, im-
precise articulation of consonants [2], and involuntary introduction of pauses [3].
Clinical observations in the speech of patients can be objectively and automati-
cally measured by using computer aided methods supported in signal processing
and pattern recognition with the aim to address two main aspects: (1) to sup-
port the diagnosis of the disease by classifying healthy control (HC) subjects and
patients, and (2) to predict the level of degradation of the speech of the patients
according to a specific clinical scale.
Most of the studies in the literature to classify PD from speech are based
on computing hand-crafted features and using classifiers such as support vector
machines (SVMs) or K-nearest neighbors (KNN). For instance, in [4],the au-
thors computed features related to perturbations of the fundamental frequency
and 20 HC subjects, Turkish speakers. Classifiers based on KNN and SVMs
were considered, and accuracies of up to 75% were reported. Later, in [5] the
authors proposed a phonation analysis based on several time frequency repre-
sentations to assess tremor in the speech of PD patients. The extracted features
were based on energy and entropy computed from time frequency representa-
tions. Several classifiers were used, including Gaussian mixture models (GMMs)
and SVMs.Accuracies of up to 77% were reported in utterances of the PC-GITA
database [6], formed with utterances from 50 PD patients and 50 HC subjects,
Colombian Spanish native speakers. The authors from [7] computed features to
model different articulation deficits in PD such as vowel quality,coordination
of laryngeal and supra-laryngeal activity, precision of consonant articulation,
tongue movement, occlusion weakening, and speech timing. The authors studied
the rapid repetition of the syllables /pa-ta-ka/ pronounced by 24 Czech native
speakers, and reported an accuracy of 88% discriminating between PD patients
and HC speakers, using an SVM classifier. Additional articulation features were
proposed in [8], where the authors modeled the difficulty of PD patients to
start/stop the vocal fold vibration in continuous speech. The model was based
on the energy content in the transitions between unvoiced and voiced segments.
The authors classified PD patients and HC speakers with speech recordings in
three different languages (Spanish, German, and Czech), and reported accuracies
ranging from 80% to 94% depending on the language; however, the results were
optimistic, since the hyper-parameters of the classifier were optimized based on
the accuracy on the test set. Another articulation model was proposed in [9]. The
authors considered a forced alignment strategy to segment the different phonetic
units in the speech utterances. The phonemes were segmented and grouped to
train different GMMs. The classification was performed based on a threshold of

CNNs and a Transfer Learning Strategy to Classify PD from Speech 3
the difference between the posterior probabilities from the models created for
HC subjects and PD patients. The model was tested with Colombian Spanish
utterances from the PC-GITA database[6] and with the Czech data from[10].
The authors reported accuracies of up to 81% for the Spanish data, and of up
to 94% for the Czech data.
In addition to the hand-crafted feature extraction models,there is a grow-
ing interest in the research community to consider deep learning models in the
assessment of the speech of PD patients [11,12,13]. Deep learning methods have
the potential to extract more abstract and robust features than those manu-
ally computed.These features could help toimprove the accuracy of different
models to classify pathological speech, such as PD [14]. A deep learning based
articulation model was proposed in [12] to model the difficulties of the patients
to stop/start the vibration of the vocal folds. Transitions between voiced and
unvoiced segments were modeled with time-frequency representations and con-
volutional neural networks (CNNs). The authors considered speech recordings of
PD patients and HC speakers in three languages: Spanish, German, and Czech,
and reported accuracies ranging from 70% to 89%, depending on the language.
However, in a language independent scenario, i.e., training the CNN with utter-
ances from one language and testing with the remaining two, the results were
not satisfactory (accuracy< 60%).
The classification of PD from speech in different languages has to be carefully
conducted to avoid bias towards the linguistic content present in each language.
For instance, Czech and German languages are richer than Spanish language
in terms of consonant production, which may cause that it is easier to produce
consonant sounds by Czech PD patients than by Spanish PD patients. Despite
these language dependent issues, the results in the classification of PD in dif-
ferent languages could be improved using a transfer learning strategy among
languages, i.e., to train a base model with utterances from one language, and
then,to perform a fine-tuning of the weights with utterances from the target
language [15]. Similar approaches based on transfer learning have been recently
considered to classify PD using handwriting [16]. In the present study, we pro-
pose a methodology to classify PD via a transfer learning strategy with the aim
to improve the accuracy in different languages. CNNs trained with utterances
from PD patients in a different language. The models are evaluated with speech
utterances in Spanish, German, and Czech languages. The results suggest that
the use of a transfer learning strategy improved the accuracy of the models over
8%with respect to those obtained when the model is trained only with utterance
from the target language.

2.1Data
Speech recordings of patients in three different languages are considered: Spanish,

2.2 2Segmentation
Speech signals are analyzed based on the automatic detection of onset and offset
transitions, which model the difficulties of the patients to start /stop the move-
ment of the vocal folds. The detection of the transitions is based on the presence
of the fundamental frequency of speech in short-time frames, as it was shown

in [8]. The border between voiced and unvoiced frames is detected, and 80 ms of
the signal are taken to the left and to the right, forming segments with 160 ms
length. The transition segments are modeled with two different approaches: (1)
a baseline model based on hand-crafted features, which are classified using an
SVM, and (2) a model based on time-frequency representations used as input to
train a CNN, which then will be used for the transfer learning strategy. Further
details are given in the following subsections.
2.3Baseline model
The features extracted from the transitions include 12 Mel-Frequency Cepstral
Coefficients (MFCCs) with their first and second derivatives, and the log energy
of the signal distributed into 22 Bark bands. The total number of descriptors
corresponds to 58. Four statistical functionals (mean,standard deviation, skew-
ness, and kurtosis) are computed for each descriptor, obtaining a 232-dimensional
feature-vector per utterance. The classification of PD patients and HC speak-
ers is performed with a radial basis SVM with margin parameter C = 10 and
a Gaussian kernel with parameter  = 0.0001. The SVM is tested following a
10-fold Cross-Validation strategy, speaker independent.
2.4CNN model
to discriminate between PD patients and HC subjects.The STFT with 256 fre-
quency bins is computed for each segmented transition, for a window length of
16 ms and a step-size of 4 ms, forming 41 time frames per transition. The ob-
tained spectrogram is transformed into the Mel-scale using 80 filters, forming
an spectrogram with a size of 80x41,which is used to train the CNNs. The
architecture of the implemented CNN is summarized in Table 2. It consists of
four convolutional and max-pooling layers, dropout to regularize the weights,
and two fully connected layers followed by the output layer to make the final
decision using a softmax activation function. The number of feature maps on
each convolutional layer is twice the previous one in order to get more detailed
representations of the input space in the deeper layers. The CNN is trained using
the the cross-entropy as the loss function, using an Adam optimizer [20].
2.5Transfer learning

in another domain.We use transfer learning to classify patients and healthy
speakers in three different languages. The CNN architecture described before is

model is used as a base to initialize two different models with the remaining

4 Conclusion
This study proposed the use of a transfer learning strategy based on fine-tuning
to classify PD from speech in three different languages: Spanish, German, and
Czech. The transfer learning among languages aimed to improve the accuracy
when the models are initialized with utterances from a different language than
the one used for the test set. Mel-scale spectrograms extracted from the transi-
tions between voiced and unvoiced segments are used to train a CNN for each
language. Then, the trained models are used to fine-tune a model to classify
utterances in the remainingtwolanguages.
The results indicate that the transfer learning among languages improved
the accuracy of the models in up to 8% when a base model trained with Spanish

utterances is used to fine-tune a model to classify PD German utterances. The
results obtained after the transfer learning are also more balanced in terms of
specificity-sensitivity and have a lower variance. In addition, the transfer learning
among languages scheme was accurate to improve the accuracy in the target
language only when the base model was robust enough. This was observed when
the model trained with Spanish utterances was used to initialize the models for
German and Czechlanguages.
Further experiments will include the development of more robust base mod-
els using hyper-parameter optimization strategies like those based on Bayesian
optimization. In addition, the base models will be trained considering two of the
languages instead of only one of them. The trained models will also be evaluated
to classify the speech of PD patients in several stages of the disease based on the
MDS-UPDRS-III score, or based on their dysarthria severity [21]. Further exper-
iments will also include transfer learning among diseases, for instance training
a base model with utterances to classify PD,and use such a model to initialize
another one to classify other neurological diseases such as Hungtinton's disease.

1 Introduction
Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the
progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the mid-brain producing several mo-
tor and non-motor impairments in the patients[1].Motor symptoms include

2 J.C.Vasquez-Correaet al.
among others, bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, micrographia, and different
speech impairments. The speech impairments observed in PD patients are typ-
ically grouped as hypokinetic dysarthria, and include symptoms such as vocal
folds rigidity, bradykinesia, and reduced control of muscles and limbs involved in
the speech production. The effects of dysarthria in the speech of PD patients in-
clude increased acoustic noise, reduced intensity, harsh and breathy voice quality,
increased voice nasality, monopitch, monoludness, speech rate disturbances, im-
precise articulation of consonants [2], and involuntary introduction of pauses [3].
Clinical observations in the speech of patients can be objectively and automati-
cally measured by using computer aided methods supported in signal processing
and pattern recognition with the aim to address two main aspects: (1) to sup-
port the diagnosis of the disease by classifying healthy control (HC) subjects and
patients, and (2) to predict the level of degradation of the speech of the patients
according to a specific clinical scale.
Most of the studies in the literature to classify PD from speech are based
on computing hand-crafted features and using classifiers such as support vector
machines (SVMs) or K-nearest neighbors (KNN). For instance, in [4],the au-
thors computed features related to perturbations of the fundamental frequency
and 20 HC subjects, Turkish speakers. Classifiers based on KNN and SVMs
were considered, and accuracies of up to 75% were reported. Later, in [5] the
authors proposed a phonation analysis based on several time frequency repre-
sentations to assess tremor in the speech of PD patients. The extracted features
were based on energy and entropy computed from time frequency representa-
tions. Several classifiers were used, including Gaussian mixture models (GMMs)
and SVMs.Accuracies of up to 77% were reported in utterances of the PC-GITA
database [6], formed with utterances from 50 PD patients and 50 HC subjects,
Colombian Spanish native speakers. The authors from [7] computed features to
model different articulation deficits in PD such as vowel quality,coordination
of laryngeal and supra-laryngeal activity, precision of consonant articulation,
tongue movement, occlusion weakening, and speech timing. The authors studied
the rapid repetition of the syllables /pa-ta-ka/ pronounced by 24 Czech native
speakers, and reported an accuracy of 88% discriminating between PD patients
and HC speakers, using an SVM classifier. Additional articulation features were
proposed in [8], where the authors modeled the difficulty of PD patients to
start/stop the vocal fold vibration in continuous speech. The model was based
on the energy content in the transitions between unvoiced and voiced segments.
The authors classified PD patients and HC speakers with speech recordings in
three different languages (Spanish, German, and Czech), and reported accuracies
ranging from 80% to 94% depending on the language; however, the results were
optimistic, since the hyper-parameters of the classifier were optimized based on
the accuracy on the test set. Another articulation model was proposed in [9]. The
authors considered a forced alignment strategy to segment the different phonetic
units in the speech utterances. The phonemes were segmented and grouped to
train different GMMs. The classification was performed based on a threshold of

CNNs and a Transfer Learning Strategy to Classify PD from Speech 3
the difference between the posterior probabilities from the models created for
HC subjects and PD patients. The model was tested with Colombian Spanish
utterances from the PC-GITA database[6] and with the Czech data from[10].
The authors reported accuracies of up to 81% for the Spanish data, and of up
to 94% for the Czech data.
In addition to the hand-crafted feature extraction models,there is a grow-
ing interest in the research community to consider deep learning models in the
assessment of the speech of PD patients [11,12,13]. Deep learning methods have
the potential to extract more abstract and robust features than those manu-
ally computed.These features could help toimprove the accuracy of different
models to classify pathological speech, such as PD [14]. A deep learning based
articulation model was proposed in [12] to model the difficulties of the patients
to stop/start the vibration of the vocal folds. Transitions between voiced and
unvoiced segments were modeled with time-frequency representations and con-
volutional neural networks (CNNs). The authors considered speech recordings of
PD patients and HC speakers in three languages: Spanish, German, and Czech,
and reported accuracies ranging from 70% to 89%, depending on the language.
However, in a language independent scenario, i.e., training the CNN with utter-
ances from one language and testing with the remaining two, the results were
not satisfactory (accuracy< 60%).
The classification of PD from speech in different languages has to be carefully
conducted to avoid bias towards the linguistic content present in each language.
For instance, Czech and German languages are richer than Spanish language
in terms of consonant production, which may cause that it is easier to produce
consonant sounds by Czech PD patients than by Spanish PD patients. Despite
these language dependent issues, the results in the classification of PD in dif-
ferent languages could be improved using a transfer learning strategy among
languages, i.e., to train a base model with utterances from one language, and
then,to perform a fine-tuning of the weights with utterances from the target
language [15]. Similar approaches based on transfer learning have been recently
considered to classify PD using handwriting [16]. In the present study, we pro-
pose a methodology to classify PD via a transfer learning strategy with the aim
to improve the accuracy in different languages. CNNs trained with utterances
from PD patients in a different language. The models are evaluated with speech
utterances in Spanish, German, and Czech languages. The results suggest that
the use of a transfer learning strategy improved the accuracy of the models over
8%with respect to those obtained when the model is trained only with utterance
from the target language.

2.2 2Segmentation
Speech signals are analyzed based on the automatic detection of onset and offset
transitions, which model the difficulties of the patients to start /stop the move-
ment of the vocal folds. The detection of the transitions is based on the presence
of the fundamental frequency of speech in short-time frames, as it was shown

in [8]. The border between voiced and unvoiced frames is detected, and 80 ms of
the signal are taken to the left and to the right, forming segments with 160 ms
length. The transition segments are modeled with two different approaches: (1)
a baseline model based on hand-crafted features, which are classified using an
SVM, and (2) a model based on time-frequency representations used as input to
train a CNN, which then will be used for the transfer learning strategy. Further
details are given in the following subsections.
2.3Baseline model
The features extracted from the transitions include 12 Mel-Frequency Cepstral
Coefficients (MFCCs) with their first and second derivatives, and the log energy
of the signal distributed into 22 Bark bands. The total number of descriptors
corresponds to 58. Four statistical functionals (mean,standard deviation, skew-
ness, and kurtosis) are computed for each descriptor, obtaining a 232-dimensional
feature-vector per utterance. The classification of PD patients and HC speak-
ers is performed with a radial basis SVM with margin parameter C = 10 and
a Gaussian kernel with parameter  = 0.0001. The SVM is tested following a
10-fold Cross-Validation strategy, speaker independent.
2.4CNN model
to discriminate between PD patients and HC subjects.The STFT with 256 fre-
quency bins is computed for each segmented transition, for a window length of
16 ms and a step-size of 4 ms, forming 41 time frames per transition. The ob-
tained spectrogram is transformed into the Mel-scale using 80 filters, forming
an spectrogram with a size of 80x41,which is used to train the CNNs. The
architecture of the implemented CNN is summarized in Table 2. It consists of
four convolutional and max-pooling layers, dropout to regularize the weights,
and two fully connected layers followed by the output layer to make the final
decision using a softmax activation function. The number of feature maps on
each convolutional layer is twice the previous one in order to get more detailed
representations of the input space in the deeper layers. The CNN is trained using
the the cross-entropy as the loss function, using an Adam optimizer [20].
2.5Transfer learning
Transfer learning allows to use a neural network trained for one task to be used
in another domain.We use transfer learning to classify patients and healthy
speakers in three different languages. The CNN architecture described before is
used to train a CNN with utterances from one language. Then, the pre-trained
model is used as a base to initialize two different models with the remaining
languages. Figure 1 summarizes this procedure.

4 Conclusion
This study proposed the use of a transfer learning strategy based on fine-tuning
to classify PD from speech in three different languages: Spanish, German, and
Czech. The transfer learning among languages aimed to improve the accuracy
when the models are initialized with utterances from a different language than
the one used for the test set. Mel-scale spectrograms extracted from the transi-
tions between voiced and unvoiced segments are used to train a CNN for each
language. Then, the trained models are used to fine-tune a model to classify
utterances in the remainingtwolanguages.
The results indicate that the transfer learning among languages improved
the accuracy of the models in up to 8% when a base model trained with Spanish

CNNs and a Transfer Learning Strategy to Classify PD from Speech 9
utterances is used to fine-tune a model to classify PD German utterances. The
results obtained after the transfer learning are also more balanced in terms of
specificity-sensitivity and have a lower variance. In addition, the transfer learning
among languages scheme was accurate to improve the accuracy in the target
language only when the base model was robust enough. This was observed when
the model trained with Spanish utterances was used to initialize the models for
German and Czechlanguages.
Further experiments will include the development of more robust base mod-
els using hyper-parameter optimization strategies like those based on Bayesian
optimization. In addition, the base models will be trained considering two of the
languages instead of only one of them. The trained models will also be evaluated
to classify the speech of PD patients in several stages of the disease based on the
MDS-UPDRS-III score, or based on their dysarthria severity [21]. Further exper-
iments will also include transfer learning among diseases, for instance training
a base model with utterances to classify PD,and use such a model to initialize
another one to classify other neurological diseases such as Hungtinton's disease.

and 20 HC subjects, Turkish speakers. Classifiers based on KNN and SVMs
were considered, and accuracies of up to 75% were reported. Later, in [5] the
authors proposed a phonation analysis based on several time frequency repre-

were based on energy and entropy computed from time frequency representa-

and SVMs.Accuracies of up to 77% were reported in utterances of the PC-GITA
database [6], formed with utterances from 50 PD patients and 50 HC subjects,
Colombian Spanish native speakers. The authors from [7] computed features to
model different articulation deficits in PD such as vowel quality,coordination
of laryngeal and supra-laryngeal activity, precision of consonant articulation,
tongue movement, occlusion weakening, and speech timing. The authors studied
the rapid repetition of the syllables /pa-ta-ka/ pronounced by 24 Czech native
speakers, and reported an accuracy of 88% discriminating between PD patients
and HC speakers, using an SVM classifier. Additional articulation features were
proposed in [8], where the authors modeled the difficulty of PD patients to
start/stop the vocal fold vibration in continuous speech. The model was based
on the energy content in the transitions between unvoiced and voiced segments.
The authors classified PD patients and HC speakers with speech recordings in
three different languages (Spanish, German, and Czech), and reported accuracies
ranging from 80% to 94% depending on the language; however, the results were

PC-GITA contains utterances from 50 PD patients and 50 HC Colombian Spanish native speakers, all of whom are native speakers of Colombian Spanish ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). This corpus provides the Spanish portion of the cross-lingual speech data and is used both for individual language classification and as a base language in transfer learning experiments ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)).

The speech tasks performed by Spanish participants include the pronunciation of a total of 10 sentences, the rapid repetition of /pa-ta-ka/, /pe-ta-ka/, /pa-ka-ta/, /pa/, /ta/, and /ka/, one text with 36 words, and a monologue ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). All Spanish PD patients were in the ON state at the time of recording, meaning they were under the effect of their daily medication ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). This is a relevant clinical detail because medication state can influence speech symptoms and thus the acoustic characteristics of the recordings.

The primary source reports demographic and clinical information for the Spanish dataset, including age ranges, mean ages, time since diagnosis, and MDS-UPDRS-III scores ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). For Spanish PD patients, the mean MDS-UPDRS-III score was 37.8 (SD = 22.1) for male patients and 37.6 (SD = 14.1) for female patients. The mean time after diagnosis was 12.6 years (SD = 11.6) for male patients and 8.7 years (SD = 5.9) for female patients ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). These values indicate that the Spanish PD cohort had comparatively higher disease severity and longer disease duration than the German and Czech cohorts, a factor that the paper later uses to explain why Spanish utterances provided the best base model for transfer learning ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

## German Dataset

The German data consist of speech recordings from 44 PD patients and 44 HC speakers ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). Unlike the Spanish PC-GITA corpus, the German dataset is not given a formal corpus name in the provided text; it is described simply as German speech recordings ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). The German dataset supplies the German portion of the cross-lingual speech data and is used for both individual language classification and transfer learning ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)).

The speech tasks performed by German participants include four tasks: the rapid repetition of /pa-ta-ka/, five sentences, one text with 81 words, and a monologue ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The primary source’s Table 1 reports demographic and clinical information for German participants, although the provided text is partially garbled. According to the table, the mean MDS-UPDRS-III score was 22.1 (SD = 9.9) for male patients and 23.3 (SD = 12.0) for female patients. The mean time after diagnosis was 7.0 years (SD = 5.5) for male patients and 7.1 years (SD = 6.2) for female patients ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). These scores are substantially lower than those of the Spanish PD cohort, indicating milder average disease severity in the German dataset ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

The German dataset is particularly important in the transfer learning experiments because the highest accuracy for German was obtained when the CNN was fine-tuned from a Spanish base model. The accuracy improved from 69.3% in the baseline model to 77.3% when the model was fine-tuned from Spanish ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). This improvement of over 8 percentage points is one of the central findings of the study and directly depends on the composition and quality of the German dataset ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

## Czech Dataset

The Czech dataset contains a total of 100 native Czech speakers, comprising 50 PD patients and 50 healthy controls ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). The Czech data are associated with the work of Rusz (2018) and prior Czech data sources cited in the paper ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The speech tasks performed by Czech participants include the rapid repetition of the syllables /pa-ta-ka/, a read text with 80 words, and a monologue ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). Like the German dataset, the Czech dataset is not presented under a formal corpus name in the provided text; it is described as Czech speech recordings ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)).

The primary source reports clinical and demographic information for the Czech PD patients as well. The mean MDS-UPDRS-III score was 21.4 (SD = 11.5) for male patients and 18.1 (SD = 9.7) for female patients. The mean time after diagnosis was 6.7 years (SD = 4.5) for male patients and 6.8 years (SD = 5.2) for female patients ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). These values are similar to the German cohort and lower than the Spanish cohort, again indicating milder average disease severity in the Czech data ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

In the experiments, the Czech dataset benefited from transfer learning when the base model was trained on Spanish utterances. The initial CNN accuracy for Czech was 68.5%, and it improved to 72.6% when the model was fine-tuned from Spanish, an improvement of over 4.1 percentage points ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). This result reinforces the role of the Spanish dataset as a robust base model for cross-lingual transfer.

## Dataset Structure and Preprocessing

Although the query focuses on which datasets are used, it is important to describe how the datasets were structured and preprocessed, because these steps define the effective data used by the models. The speech signals from all three datasets were analyzed based on the automatic detection of onset and offset transitions, which model the difficulties of patients in starting and stopping the movement of the vocal folds ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The detection of transitions is based on the presence of the fundamental frequency of speech in short-time frames ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The border between voiced and unvoiced frames is detected, and 80 ms of the signal are taken to the left and to the right, forming segments with 160 ms length ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

Two modeling approaches were applied to these transition segments. The baseline model used hand-crafted features: 12 Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) with their first and second derivatives, and the log energy of the signal distributed into 22 Bark bands, yielding 58 descriptors ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). Four statistical functionals—mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis—were computed for each descriptor, producing a 232-dimensional feature vector per utterance ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The CNN model, by contrast, used time-frequency representations. A short-time Fourier transform (STFT) with 256 frequency bins was computed for each segmented transition, using a window length of 16 ms and a step size of 4 ms, forming 41 time frames per transition ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The resulting spectrogram was transformed into the Mel scale using 80 filters, producing an 80×41 spectrogram that was used to train the CNNs ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

For the final decision per speaker, a majority voting strategy was applied across the different speech exercises performed by each participant ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). This means that the datasets were not used as isolated utterance-level samples alone; instead, the speaker-level classification was derived from multiple tasks per speaker, which is an important characteristic of the dataset design.

The tasks are similar in that they include rapid syllable repetition, read speech, and monologue. The use of multiple tasks per speaker is nevertheless a strength, because it allows the majority voting strategy to combine evidence across different speech conditions.

## Use of the Datasets in Experiments

The datasets are used in two main experimental stages. First, baseline and CNN models are trained considering each language individually ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). Second, the trained CNNs for each language are used as base models in a transfer learning strategy to improve accuracy in the other two languages ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). In other words, the Spanish, German, and Czech datasets are not only separate evaluation sets; they are also sources of pre-trained weights for cross-lingual adaptation ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

The results show that the Spanish dataset produced the most robust base model. When the Spanish model was used to initialize the German model, accuracy improved from 69.3% in the baseline to 77.3% ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). When the Spanish model was used to initialize the Czech model, accuracy improved from 68.5% to 72.6% ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The paper concludes that the transfer learning among languages improved accuracy in up to 8% when the base model used to initialize the weights of the classifier was robust enough ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The Spanish dataset, with its higher disease severity and better initial separability, fulfilled this condition ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

The datasets also differ in how balanced the classification results are in terms of sensitivity and specificity. The paper notes that for the three languages, the results without transfer learning were unbalanced toward one of the two classes according to specificity and sensitivity values ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). After transfer learning, the results were in most cases more balanced, and the standard deviation of the transferred CNNs was lower, which the authors interpret as an improvement in generalization ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). This suggests that the dataset composition and cross-lingual transfer interact in ways that affect not only overall accuracy but also the balance between true positive and true negative rates.

## Data Quality, Limitations, and Reliability

The three datasets have several strengths. They are multi-language, include balanced numbers of PD and HC speakers, and involve clinical evaluation by a neurologist expert using MDS-UPDRS-III ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). The recordings were captured in noise-controlled conditions and down-sampled to 16 kHz, which supports reproducibility and comparability ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The use of multiple speech tasks per speaker and majority voting at the speaker level further strengthens the dataset design ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

However, there are also limitations and data quality issues. First, the German and Czech datasets are not given formal corpus names in the provided text, unlike the Spanish PC-GITA corpus ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt); [Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). This makes it harder to trace the exact provenance of those data from the provided information alone. Second, the primary source’s Table 1 has formatting problems in the provided text, including ambiguous counts for the German speakers ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The third-party research note helps resolve this by explicitly stating that the German data contain 44 PD patients and 44 HC speakers ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). Third, the paper contains a minor inconsistency in labeling the clinical scale as MDS-UPDRS-II in one passage, while the third section of the scale is MDS-UPDRS-III and the research note uses MDS-UPDRS-III ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt); [Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). Fourth, the datasets differ in disease severity and task protocols, which may confound cross-lingual comparisons ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). Finally, the transfer learning approach only improved accuracy when the base model was robust enough, which means that not all datasets function equally well as source domains ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)).

In terms of reliability, the primary source is an arXiv preprint by Vasquez-Correa et al. (2020), and the third-party note is a research summary that aligns with the primary source’s main dataset counts ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt); [Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). The PC-GITA corpus is a known Spanish speech corpus for Parkinson’s disease research, and the Czech data are linked to established work by Rusz and colleagues ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The German data are described in sufficient detail to understand their composition, even without a formal corpus name ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). Overall, the datasets are appropriate for the study’s aims, but readers should be aware of the reporting inconsistencies and the lack of formal names for two of the three datasets.

## Conclusion

The study by Vasquez-Correa et al. (2020) uses three language-specific speech datasets: the Spanish PC-GITA corpus, German speech recordings, and Czech speech recordings ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt); [Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). The Spanish dataset comprises 50 PD patients and 50 HC Colombian Spanish native speakers; the German dataset comprises 44 PD patients and 44 HC speakers; and the Czech dataset comprises 50 PD patients and 50 HC native Czech speakers ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). Across all three datasets, the study includes 144 PD patients and 144 healthy controls, totaling 288 speakers. The datasets were evaluated clinically with MDS-UPDRS-III, recorded in noise-controlled conditions, down-sampled to 16 kHz, and processed into voiced/unvoiced transition segments for CNN and baseline modeling ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The Spanish PC-GITA corpus is the most clearly named and documented dataset, and it also served as the most effective base model for cross-lingual transfer learning, improving German accuracy to 77.3% and Czech accuracy to 72.6% ([Vasquez-Correa et al., 2020](document_1.txt)). The German and Czech datasets are described by speaker counts and task protocols rather than formal corpus names in the provided text, and the primary source contains some table formatting inconsistencies that the third-party note helps clarify ([Third-party research note, n.d.](document_2.txt)). These three datasets form the empirical foundation for the paper’s conclusions about CNN-based Parkinson’s disease classification from speech and cross-lingual transfer learning.
